text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game variant where keeping a token in my own account gives me +1 but costs each of the other three members 0.3 points, while putting a token in the group account only gives me +0.3 and doesn't affect others at all.

Individually, keeping dominates since 1 > 0.3 regardless of what others do, but socially the group is worse off since keeping creates a net negative externality (1 - 0.9 = 0.1) compared to contributing's clean 0.3. This is a classic social dilemma, and since it repeats over 10 rounds, cooperation could potentially be sustained through reciprocity or reputation effects even though each round's dominant strategy is to defect.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure of this public goods game, factoring in my kept tokens versus contributions to the group account and how the negative externality on others' kept tokens affects my score.

So the math shows keeping all tokens is each player's dominant strategy, since keeping yields +1 to me but only -0.9 externality to others, while contributing yields just +0.3 to me versus +1.2 total welfare if everyone contributes. That means individual incentives push toward everyone hoarding even though full cooperation would maximize group welfare -- classic tension between Nash equilibrium and social optimum across the ten repeated rounds.
